summary:
Sean DuBois (OpenAI, WebRTC, Realtime API, 1-800-CHATGPT, founder of Pion) and Kwindla Kramer (Daily, Pipecat) deliver a talk on building natural, fast, humanlike voice experiences, stressing that latency is the dominant concern—nothing else matters if the AI responds too slowly. They target ~500ms voice-to-voice latency (time from human stops talking to first audio byte from LLM) as natural-sounding, with >1 second causing low completion rates, low NPS, and hang-ups. A real-world latency breakdown from a browser-based voice app talking to a Pipecat cloud agent shows just under one second—good but improvable with trade-offs in quality or cost.

The central technical argument is that WebSockets, being TCP-based, guarantee in-order delivery and block on packet loss, causing audio glitchiness, high latency, or disconnections in 10-15% of real-world connections. WebRTC, by contrast, uses clever math and buffer management to ignore stale packets within a tight latency budget—"super fast, best effort networking." WebRTC also provides built-in resampling, packetization, bandwidth estimation, and standard stats/observability APIs that WebSockets users must build themselves. The TL;DR: use WebSockets for server-to-server and small structured data or prototyping; use WebRTC for audio/video streams over the internet. WebRTC powers Messenger, WhatsApp, Zoom, Discord, and novel applications like internet-based surgery and teleoperated vehicles.

The speakers frame voice as the core building block of next-generation UIs for the generative AI era, drawing an analogy to late 2007—first iPhones exist but pull-to-refresh hasn't been invented yet. A live demo features "Squabbert," a Raspberry Pi connected peer-to-peer via WebRTC to a laptop over LAN, running MLX, Whisper, Gemma 3, and a custom logic sampler. The talk emphasizes WebRTC's flexibility in offering multiple connection topologies: local peer-to-peer, cloud-relayed, or multi-party via Pipecat to bring LLMs into meetings. The talk closes with a community showcase: Yashin, a non-technical mom of bilingual kids, built a Mandarin language-learning voice app for children with community guidance—never having written code before. This underscores the speakers' thesis that accessible voice AI tooling will unlock innovation from non-traditional builders.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Opening and Introductions
sections.summary: The talk opens with a scripted comedic conversation between Sean and Squabbert (a voice AI device) about the risks of a live demo. Sean introduces himself as working on WebRTC at OpenAI (Realtime API, 1-800-CHATGPT, Pion). Kwin introduces himself as working at Daily on realtime infrastructure and the open-source Pipecat voice agent framework. They announce the topic: building natural, fast, humanlike voice experiences with a crash course on low-latency audio and video.

sections.title: Latency in Voice AI
sections.summary: The speakers emphasize that latency is the dominant concern in voice AI. Around 500ms sounds natural; above 1 second leads to low completion rates, low NPS, and hang-ups. Voice-to-voice latency is defined as the time between when a human stops talking and the first audio byte returns from the LLM. A real-world latency breakdown from a browser-based Mac OS app talking to a Pipecat cloud agent shows just under 1 second—good but improvable with trade-offs. Bluetooth is called out as a major latency source.

sections.title: WebRTC vs WebSockets
sections.summary: The core technical argument: WebSockets are TCP connections guaranteeing in-order delivery, which blocks on packet loss—wrong for realtime audio. WebRTC uses clever math and buffer management to ignore stale packets within tight latency budgets, providing best-effort networking impossible to implement on TCP. WebSockets cause audio problems in 10-15% of real-world connections. WebRTC also provides built-in resampling, packetization, bandwidth estimation, and stats APIs. TL;DR: WebSockets for server-to-server/prototyping; WebRTC for edge-to-cloud audio/video. Code comparison shown using OpenAI Realtime API with both options.

sections.title: Applications and Future of Voice UI
sections.summary: WebRTC can embed realtime audio in any app (web, iOS, Android) and already powers Messenger, WhatsApp, Zoom, Discord. Novel uses include internet-based surgery and teleoperated vehicles. The speakers argue voice is the core building block of next-gen UIs for the generative AI era, drawing an analogy to late 2007—iPhones exist but pull-to-refresh hasn't been invented. Voice is described as the next 'bicycle for the mind,' enabling interaction when hands are unavailable and keeping compute power remote.

sections.title: Squabbert Demo and WebRTC Flexibility
sections.summary: Squabbert, a Raspberry Pi built by Chad and named by Chad's daughter Ella, is introduced. It runs MLX, Whisper, Gemma 3, and a custom logic sampler by Kwin. The demo includes syllable counting (described as the 2025 version of 'how many Rs in strawberry') and an attempted four-line poem using only two-syllable words (partial success). Squabbert was connected peer-to-peer via WebRTC directly to the laptop over LAN—a serverless connection. The segment ends by noting WebRTC's flexibility in connection topologies.

sections.title: Community Showcase and Call to Action
sections.summary: The speakers outline three WebRTC connection options: local peer-to-peer (like Squabbert), cloud-relayed to a server running AI, and multi-party via Pipecat to bring LLMs into meetings. They then showcase Yashin, a non-technical mom of bilingual kids who built a Mandarin language-learning voice app for children with community guidance—having never written code before. A short demo video shows a voice-guided Mandarin greeting exercise. The talk closes with a call to action: QR codes for Yashin's project and general resources, encouragement to find the speakers online (Discord, Twitter, LinkedIn), mention of Kwin's book in conference bags, and an appeal to both experienced programmers and newcomers to build the next generation of voice AI projects using tools like Pipecat and Pion.
